title: Visual Retrieval Heads: 2% of Attention Does the Grounding
hook: VLMs point at the right part of an image through a tiny set of attention heads — mask the top 20 and grounding accuracy drops by up to 80 points.
key_points: Visual Retrieval Heads (VRHs) are about 1.7-2.6% of attention heads and are causally responsible for grounding text to image regions.
Best identification method: score attention from output prediction tokens, summed over the ground-truth referent region.
Across eleven VLMs and five referring-expression benchmarks, masking the top 20 VRHs cuts grounding accuracy by up to 80 points; masking random heads barely matters.
VRHs generalize beyond how they were found — still causal on attribute, spatial, counting, and visual-math tasks despite discovery via bounding boxes.
They are functionally specific: ablation corrupts localization while preserving output format.
They are architecturally shared, transferring causally across VLMs with the same LLM backbone but different vision encoders, projectors, and instruction tuning.
content_html: Text-only LLMs have retrieval heads: a small set of attention heads causally responsible for fetching a specific fact out of context. Park and colleagues ask whether vision-language models have the same thing for images, and answer yes.
extra_html:
Finding them

The paper recasts existing head-scoring methods into a unified design space over query tokens, key aggregation, and cross-sample aggregation — then asks which point in that space actually finds causal heads. The winner: score attention from the output prediction tokens, summed over the ground-truth referent region.

That identifies Visual Retrieval Heads, roughly 1.7-2.6% of all attention heads. Across eleven VLMs and five referring-expression benchmarks, masking just the top 20 reduces grounding accuracy by up to 80 percentage points, while masking the same number of random heads has little effect.

Three properties beyond the text analogue

The text literature established that retrieval heads are causal, sparse, and universal. VRHs add three findings. They generalize — discovered through bounding-box prediction, they remain causal on attribute, spatial, counting, and visual-math benchmarks. They are functionally specific — ablating them corrupts localization while leaving output format intact, so the model still answers, just about the wrong region. And they are architecturally shared, transferring causally across VLMs that share an LLM backbone but differ in vision encoder, projector, and instruction tuning.

That last one is the most suggestive: it points at the language model, not the vision tower, as the seat of visual grounding.

related.title: Circuit Condensation: Train the Circuit Smaller
related.hook: Circuit discovery on a frozen model returns hundreds of edges nobody can check. Post-train the model to route the behavior through fewer, and circuits shrink 8x on average — up to 316x.

flashcards.prompt: What makes the random-head control essential to this result?
flashcards.back_html: It separates "these heads matter" from "removing any 20 heads hurts." Masking the top 20 VRHs drops grounding accuracy by up to 80 points; masking the same number of random heads has little effect.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean that VRHs are 'architecturally shared'?

choices.text: They transfer causally across VLMs that share an LLM backbone but differ in vision encoder, projector, and tuning
Every VLM has them in exactly the same layer index
They are copied explicitly during distillation

flashcards.explanation_html: The shared factor is the language backbone, not the visual front end — which suggests the grounding mechanism lives in the LLM rather than the vision tower.

flashcards.prompt: Why is it notable that VRHs found via bounding-box prediction stay causal on counting and visual-math tasks?
flashcards.back_html: It shows they are a general visual-reference mechanism rather than an artifact of the discovery task — the heads generalize beyond the objective used to find them.
